HomeLens AI: NLP-Based Business Risk Intelligence for Home-Service Providers¶

Exploratory Data Analysis — Course Project Milestone 2¶

Course: CIS 509 — Analytics for Unstructured Data
Team ID: HomeLensAI
Team Members: Rithik Roy Thati • Kanha Jodhpurkar • Sankalp Sharma Madgula • Dev Bhattacharyya

Submission note: The assignment requires this executed notebook and its matching HTML export. If Canvas lists a separate numeric Team ID, replace HomeLensAI in the heading and file names before submission.

Project purpose¶

Home-service companies depend heavily on customer trust, referrals, online reputation, and repeat business. This project examines whether unstructured Yelp review text can reveal recurring operational and reputational business-risk signals involving workmanship, reliability, timeliness, pricing, communication, professionalism, warranties, and safety-related complaints.

The analysis intentionally does not claim to predict bankruptcy, legal liability, or verified safety violations. It detects review-based signals that may justify management attention.

6. Preliminary Data Exploration (25%) NLTK tokenization and n-grams, TextBlob sentiment, spaCy phrase matching, NMF topics, temporal patterns, business-level summaries, and a leakage-aware TF-IDF baseline.

The notebook follows the required story: business problem → data → exploratory findings → proposed AI solution.

2. Project Overview (10%)¶

Business problem¶

Home-service providers—including contractors, plumbers, HVAC companies, roofers, movers, cleaners, property managers, electricians, and repair companies—receive large volumes of customer feedback. Important concerns can be hidden in free-form text and may not be visible from an average star rating alone. A manager needs to know what went wrong, whether the issue is recurring, whether complaint frequency is changing, and which problem deserves attention first.

Main business question¶

Can natural-language processing identify, classify, and explain operational and reputational business-risk signals in Yelp reviews of home-service providers so managers can prioritize corrective action?

Stakeholders¶

Primary users are home-service business owners, operations managers, quality-control teams, customer-experience teams, regional managers, reputation-management teams, and safety or compliance personnel. Customers are secondary beneficiaries because faster identification of recurring problems can improve service quality.

Analytical goals¶

  1. Describe the text corpus and assess whether it is suitable for NLP.
  2. Examine sentiment, vocabulary, phrases, service categories, time trends, and complaint themes.
  3. Use NLTK and spaCy for preliminary text processing and risk-aspect extraction.
  4. Test whether review language contains enough signal for supervised classification.
  5. Design a next-stage AI solution that combines transformer sentiment classification, explainable issue detection, and business-level monitoring.

Scope refinement¶

The Milestone 1 concept centered on multimodal real-estate valuation. After confirming that this course project must make meaningful use of unstructured language, the team refined HomeLens AI toward business-risk intelligence for the home-services industry. The housing-domain identity remains, while the project now directly applies the course's NLP methods to substantial free-form text.

3. Data Sources (10%)¶

Original source¶

The derived project file comes from the Yelp Open Dataset, which provides newline-delimited JSON files for businesses and reviews.

  • Official dataset page: https://business.yelp.com/data/resources/open-dataset/
  • Official documentation: https://www.yelp.com/dataset/documentation/main
  • Kaggle mirror used to create the smaller project file: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/yelp-dataset/yelp-dataset

Source files and join¶

  • yelp_academic_dataset_business.json: business name, location, categories, overall rating, and review count.
  • yelp_academic_dataset_review.json: review identifiers, star rating, date, engagement counts, and free-form text.
  • Join key: business_id.

How the project CSV was collected and selected¶

  1. Candidate businesses were selected when the Yelp categories field contained a home-related service term.
  2. The city-state market with the largest candidate home-service presence in the extraction was selected; the resulting file contains Tucson, Arizona.
  3. The large review JSON was read in chunks, keeping only reviews whose business_id matched a selected business.
  4. Reviews were joined to business metadata, blank text and duplicate review IDs were removed, and the result was exported as HomeLens_Yelp_HomeServices.csv.
  5. This notebook applies a second, documented core-provider filter to remove adjacent retail, hotel, apartment-only, and automotive records that entered through broad Yelp categories.

The primary unstructured variable is text. Converting the JSON records to CSV does not make the review language structured; the free-form text remains unstructured.

Analytical selection: core home-service providers¶

Yelp categories are multi-label and broad. The candidate file includes some retailers, hotels, apartment-only listings, utilities, and automotive businesses because they also carried a generic Home Services or real-estate category. The following rules retain businesses with at least one clearly operational home-service category, then remove obvious hotel, apartment-only, and primarily automotive records.

This refinement is part of the analysis—not an attempt to make results look better. It makes the business population match the stated decision problem.

In [6]:
def parse_categories(value):
    return {item.strip() for item in str(value).split(",") if item.strip()}

CORE_CATEGORIES = {
    "Contractors", "General Contractors", "Plumbing",
    "Heating & Air Conditioning/HVAC", "Water Heater Installation/Repair",
    "Electricians", "Roofing", "Landscaping", "Landscape Architects",
    "Gardeners", "Tree Services", "Irrigation", "Lawn Services", "Painters",
    "Flooring", "Tiling", "Carpeting", "Carpet Installation", "Carpet Cleaning",
    "Home Cleaning", "Office Cleaning", "Window Washing", "Pressure Washers",
    "Pest Control", "Pool & Hot Tub Service", "Pool Cleaners", "Swimming Pools",
    "Damage Restoration", "Garage Door Services", "Door Sales/Installation",
    "Windows Installation", "Glass & Mirrors", "Keys & Locksmiths",
    "Security Systems", "Solar Installation", "Home Inspectors", "Handyman",
    "Fences & Gates", "Masonry/Concrete", "Septic Services",
    "Water Purification Services", "Appliances & Repair", "Junk Removal & Hauling",
    "Movers", "Packing Services", "Property Management", "Cabinetry",
    "Countertop Installation", "Kitchen & Bath", "Drywall Installation & Repair",
    "Stucco Services", "Refinishing Services", "Home Organization", "Interior Design",
    "Home Theatre Installation", "Air Duct Cleaning", "Hydro-jetting",
    "Grout Services", "Shades & Blinds", "Shutters",
    "Lighting Fixtures & Equipment", "Furniture Reupholstery", "Metal Fabricators"
}

category_sets = raw_df["categories"].apply(parse_categories)

core_mask = category_sets.apply(lambda values: bool(values & CORE_CATEGORIES))
core_mask &= ~category_sets.apply(lambda values: bool(values & {"Hotels", "Hotels & Travel"}))
core_mask &= ~category_sets.apply(
    lambda values: "Automotive" in values
    and not bool(values & {"Movers", "Junk Removal & Hauling", "Keys & Locksmiths"})
)
core_mask &= ~category_sets.apply(
    lambda values: "Apartments" in values and "Property Management" not in values
)

df = raw_df.loc[core_mask].copy()
df["category_set"] = category_sets.loc[core_mask]

selection_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Stage": ["Candidate extracted Yelp reviews", "Core analytical subset", "Removed as adjacent/non-core"],
    "Reviews": [len(raw_df), len(df), len(raw_df) - len(df)],
    "Businesses": [raw_df["business_id"].nunique(), df["business_id"].nunique(),
                   raw_df.loc[~core_mask, "business_id"].nunique()],
})
selection_table["Share of candidate reviews"] = selection_table["Reviews"] / len(raw_df)
display(selection_table)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5))
plt.bar(selection_table["Stage"].iloc[:2], selection_table["Reviews"].iloc[:2])
plt.ylabel("Reviews")
plt.title("Candidate corpus and core home-service analytical subset")
plt.xticks(rotation=10, ha="right")
plt.tight_layout()

def assign_service_group(category_set):
    for group_name, group_categories in SERVICE_GROUPS:
        if category_set & group_categories:
            return group_name
    return "Other Core Home Services"

df["service_group"] = df["category_set"].apply(assign_service_group)

# Anonymized provider codes are used in displayed business-level tables.
provider_map = {
    business_id: f"Provider_{number:04d}"
    for number, business_id in enumerate(sorted(df["business_id"].unique()), start=1)
}
df["provider_code"] = df["business_id"].map(provider_map)

print(f"Unique reviewers retained: {df['user_id'].nunique():,}")

Interpretation¶

The corpus is strongly bimodal: five-star and one-star reviews dominate. This is useful for detecting clear positive and negative language, but the neutral class is small. For the preliminary supervised baseline, the notebook therefore uses a business-aligned binary target—1–2 stars = negative risk signal; 4–5 stars = positive/no immediate risk signal—and retains three-star reviews for descriptive analysis and later mixed-sentiment error analysis.

In [11]:
# NLTK tokenization and spaCy sentence segmentation
word_tokenizer = RegexpTokenizer(r"[A-Za-z]+(?:'[A-Za-z]+)?")
stemmer = SnowballStemmer("english")

def tokenize_words(text):
    return word_tokenizer.tokenize(str(text).lower())

df["character_count"] = df["text"].astype(str).str.len()
df["word_count"] = df["text"].apply(lambda text: len(tokenize_words(text)))

nlp_sentences = spacy.blank("en")
nlp_sentences.add_pipe("sentencizer")
df["sentence_count"] = [
    sum(1 for _ in document.sents)
    for document in nlp_sentences.pipe(df["text"].astype(str), batch_size=256)
]

document_stats = df[["character_count", "word_count", "sentence_count"]].describe(
    percentiles=[0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99]
).T

display(document_stats)

all_tokens = []
for review_text in df["text"]:
    all_tokens.extend(tokenize_words(review_text))

content_tokens = [
    token for token in all_tokens
    if len(token) > 2 and token not in STOP_WORDS
]

text_corpus_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Measure": [
        "Total word tokens", "Raw vocabulary size", "Content-word vocabulary size",
        "Median words per review", "Mean words per review", "Median sentences per review"
    ],
    "Value": [
        f"{len(all_tokens):,}", f"{len(set(all_tokens)):,}", f"{len(set(content_tokens)):,}",
        f"{df['word_count'].median():,.0f}", f"{df['word_count'].mean():,.1f}",
        f"{df['sentence_count'].median():,.0f}"
    ]
})

NLTK keyword and n-gram exploration¶

The following analysis uses NLTK's regular-expression tokenizer and bigrams. Stop words are removed with spaCy's English stop-word list so that the displayed terms emphasize business content rather than grammar words. Stemming is available for later modeling, but readable words are retained in the exploratory charts.

In [13]:
def content_word_list(text):
    return [
        token for token in tokenize_words(text)
        if len(token) > 2 and token not in STOP_WORDS
    ]

def top_terms_for_label(label, n=18):
    counter = Counter()
    for review_text in df.loc[df["sentiment_label"] == label, "text"]:
        counter.update(content_word_list(review_text))
    return pd.DataFrame(counter.most_common(n), columns=["term", "count"])

def top_bigrams_for_label(label, n=18):
    counter = Counter()
    for review_text in df.loc[df["sentiment_label"] == label, "text"]:
        tokens = content_word_list(review_text)
        counter.update(" ".join(pair) for pair in bigrams(tokens))
    return pd.DataFrame(counter.most_common(n), columns=["bigram", "count"])

negative_terms = top_terms_for_label("negative")
positive_terms = top_terms_for_label("positive")
negative_bigrams = top_bigrams_for_label("negative")
positive_bigrams = top_bigrams_for_label("positive")

print("Most common negative-review content words")
display(negative_terms)
print("Most common positive-review content words")
display(positive_terms)

Interpretation¶

Interpretation¶

Observed complaint rates differ considerably by service group. These are descriptive associations, not causal quality judgments. Property-management reviews, for example, may reflect ongoing tenant-landlord conflicts and stronger self-selection than one-time repair services. The final system should therefore compare a provider with similar businesses and should not use one universal threshold without context.

5. Data Quality and Suitability (20%)¶

Why the data are suitable¶

  • The analytical subset contains a large collection of long, natural-language documents and thousands of negative examples.
  • Reviews include outcomes, explanations, emotions, service events, timing, prices, staff behavior, and follow-up experiences that are not captured by an average rating alone.
  • Business metadata allows industry grouping, business-level aggregation, and time-based monitoring.
  • The corpus supports multiple course methods: NLTK tokenization and n-grams, TextBlob sentiment, spaCy rule matching, TF-IDF, topic modeling, and later transformer fine-tuning.

Important limitations and potential biases¶

  1. Geographic scope: the file contains Tucson, Arizona, so results may not generalize to other markets.
  2. Historical period: reviews extend through January 2022 and do not represent current 2026 conditions.
  3. Self-selection: people who post reviews may differ from customers who do not, and extreme experiences may be overrepresented.
  4. Weak labels: star ratings are practical sentiment labels, but text can be mixed, sarcastic, or inconsistent with the rating.
  5. Uneven business coverage: some providers have many reviews and others have few; business-level conclusions require a minimum review threshold and uncertainty adjustment.
  6. Category overlap: Yelp categories are multi-label, requiring transparent inclusion and exclusion rules.
  7. Complaint verification: allegations in reviews are not verified facts. A safety phrase is a safety-related complaint signal, not proof of a violation.
  8. PII and credentials: review text can contain phone numbers, email addresses, or URLs. These should be masked before modeling and should not be reproduced in reports.
  9. Target leakage: some reviewers write explicit phrases such as “one star” or “five stars.” These phrases must be masked in a star-derived sentiment model.
  10. Temporal incompleteness: January 2022 is only a partial year and should not be compared directly with full years.

Preparation and analysis challenges¶

  • Negation, sarcasm, misspellings, long narratives, and domain-specific terms complicate sentiment analysis.
  • A random row split could leak provider-specific language into the test set; the preliminary model therefore holds out entire businesses.
  • Exact duplicate text is small but is removed from supervised modeling.
  • The neutral class is limited, so binary risk classification is the most stable first supervised task.

Privacy and target-leakage audit¶

The audit below identifies text patterns that need masking before supervised modeling. Money references are useful to pricing-risk analysis, so the exact value is replaced with a generic token rather than deleting the entire phrase.

In [16]:
AUDIT_PATTERNS = {
    "Explicit star-rating phrase": r"\b(?:zero|one|two|three|four|five|first|second|third|fourth|fifth|[0-5](?:st|nd|rd|th)?)[- ]?star(?:s)?\b",
    "Phone number": r"\b(?:\+?1[-.\s]?)?\(?\d{3}\)?[-.\s]\d{3}[-.\s]\d{4}\b",
    "Email address": r"\b[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}\b",
    "URL": r"(?:https?://|www\.)\S+",
    "Currency amount": r"\$\s?\d[\d,]*(?:\.\d{2})?",
}

audit_rows = []
for pattern_name, pattern in AUDIT_PATTERNS.items():
    matched = df["text"].str.contains(pattern, case=False, regex=True, na=False)
    audit_rows.append({
        "pattern": pattern_name,
        "reviews": int(matched.sum()),
        "percent": float(matched.mean()),
    })

audit_table = pd.DataFrame(audit_rows).sort_values("reviews", ascending=False)

MASKING_RULES = [
    (r"(?:https?://|www\.)\S+", " URLTOKEN "),
    (r"\b[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}\b", " EMAILTOKEN "),
    (r"\b(?:\+?1[-.\s]?)?\(?\d{3}\)?[-.\s]\d{3}[-.\s]\d{4}\b", " PHONETOKEN "),
    (r"\$\s?\d[\d,]*(?:\.\d{2})?", " MONEYTOKEN "),
    (r"\b(?:zero|one|two|three|four|five|first|second|third|fourth|fifth|[0-5](?:st|nd|rd|th)?)[- ]?star(?:s)?\b", " RATINGTOKEN "),
]

def mask_sensitive_and_leakage(text):
    cleaned = str(text)
    for pattern, replacement in MASKING_RULES:
        cleaned = re.sub(pattern, replacement, cleaned, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", cleaned).strip()

df["model_text"] = df["text"].apply(mask_sensitive_and_leakage)

# Demonstrate the transformation without exposing full reviews or provider names.
masking_demo = pd.DataFrame({
    "original_excerpt": df["text"].head(3).str.slice(0, 180),
    "masked_excerpt": df["model_text"].head(3).str.slice(0, 180),
})

6. Preliminary Data Exploration (25%)¶

6.1 Lexicon-based sentiment benchmark with TextBlob¶

Interpretation¶

The lexicon score moves in the expected direction as stars increase, but it misses many negative reviews. Home-service complaints frequently contain long narratives, negation, mixed praise and criticism, or factual descriptions whose risk comes from context rather than strongly negative adjectives. This supports comparing a trained TF-IDF classifier and a contextual transformer with the lexicon baseline.

6.2 spaCy rule-based extraction of business-risk aspects¶

A blank English spaCy pipeline is sufficient for reliable tokenization, sentence boundaries, and PhraseMatcher patterns. The phrase dictionary is intentionally transparent and should be refined through manual review. Each match indicates a review signal, not a verified event.

In [20]:
RISK_PHRASES = {
    "Workmanship": [
        "poor quality", "bad job", "terrible job", "sloppy work", "unfinished work",
        "not finished", "installed incorrectly", "incorrect installation", "repair failed",
        "did not fix", "didn't fix", "still leaking", "stopped working", "made it worse",
        "broke again", "poor workmanship", "damaged the", "damaged my"
    ],

        "no show", "never showed", "did not show", "didn't show", "never came",
        "did not come", "didn't come", "missed appointment", "cancelled appointment",
        "canceled appointment", "failed to arrive"
    ],
    "Timeliness": [
        "arrived late", "showed up late", "hours late", "days late", "project delayed",
        "missed deadline", "took weeks", "took months", "long wait", "still waiting",
        "slow service"
    ],
    "Pricing / Billing": [

    "Communication": [

        "never responded", "did not respond", "didn't respond", "stopped responding",

        "wouldn't return my call"
    ],
    "Professionalism / Trust": [

    ],

        "water damage", "flooded my", "damaged my property", "mold problem", "safety issue"
    ],

        "wouldn't fix", "follow up repair", "follow-up repair", "return visit",
        "under warranty", "warranty claim"
    ],
}

nlp_matcher = spacy.blank("en")
nlp_matcher.add_pipe("sentencizer")
phrase_matcher = PhraseMatcher(nlp_matcher.vocab, attr="LOWER")

for aspect, phrases in RISK_PHRASES.items():
    phrase_matcher.add(aspect, [nlp_matcher.make_doc(phrase) for phrase in phrases])

aspect_columns = []
for aspect in RISK_PHRASES:
    column = "aspect_" + re.sub(r"\W+", "_", aspect.lower()).strip("_")
    aspect_columns.append(column)
    df[column] = False

for row_index, document in zip(df.index, nlp_matcher.pipe(df["text"].astype(str), batch_size=256)):
    matched_aspects = {nlp_matcher.vocab.strings[match_id] for match_id, _, _ in phrase_matcher(document)}
    for aspect in matched_aspects:
        column = "aspect_" + re.sub(r"\W+", "_", aspect.lower()).strip("_")
        df.at[row_index, column] = True

aspect_rows = []
for aspect in RISK_PHRASES:
    column = "aspect_" + re.sub(r"\W+", "_", aspect.lower()).strip("_")
    mentions = int(df[column].sum())
    negative_mentions = int((df[column] & (df["review_stars"] <= 2)).sum())
    aspect_rows.append({
        "aspect": aspect,
        "reviews_with_signal": mentions,
        "negative_reviews_with_signal": negative_mentions,
        "negative_rate_when_mentioned": negative_mentions / mentions if mentions else np.nan,
    })

aspect_summary = pd.DataFrame(aspect_rows).sort_values("reviews_with_signal", ascending=False)
display(aspect_summary)

def first_masked_example(aspect_name):

Interpretation¶

Professionalism/trust, communication, reliability/no-show, and timeliness phrases are especially concentrated in low-star reviews. Workmanship, pricing, warranties, and safety-related language also appear, but simple phrase rules cannot capture every paraphrase or determine whether an allegation is true. The next stage should validate these rules against a human-coded sample before they are used operationally.

6.3 Topic discovery within negative reviews¶

Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) is applied only to 1–2 star reviews. TF-IDF reduces common language and allows recurring complaint themes to emerge without assigning labels in advance.

In [23]:
negative_reviews = df[df["review_stars"] <= 2].copy()

topic_stop_words = sorted(
    {word for word in STOP_WORDS if word.isalpha()}
    | {
        "business", "company", "service", "services", "called", "call", "said",
        "told", "would", "could", "one", "get", "got", "time", "work", "use",
        "used", "also", "back", "even", "really"
    }
)

topic_vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(
    stop_words=topic_stop_words,
    min_df=8,
    max_df=0.75,
    max_features=5000,
    ngram_range=(1, 2),
    sublinear_tf=True,
)
negative_tfidf = topic_vectorizer.fit_transform(negative_reviews["model_text"])

nmf_model = NMF(
    n_components=6,
    init="nndsvda",
    random_state=RANDOM_SEED,
    max_iter=400,
)
topic_weights = nmf_model.fit_transform(negative_tfidf)
topic_terms = np.array(topic_vectorizer.get_feature_names_out())

TOPIC_LABELS = {
    1: "Work, cleaning, and moving outcomes",
    2: "Property management and lease disputes",
    3: "Scheduling, appointments, and follow-up",
    4: "Warranty, equipment, and repair failure",
    5: "Customer service and professionalism",
    6: "Pricing, estimates, and billing",
}

topic_rows = []
for topic_number, component in enumerate(nmf_model.components_, start=1):
    top_words = topic_terms[component.argsort()[-12:][::-1]]
    topic_rows.append({
        "topic": topic_number,
        "interpretive_label": TOPIC_LABELS[topic_number],
        "top_terms": ", ".join(top_words),
    })

topic_table = pd.DataFrame(topic_rows)
display(topic_table)

negative_reviews["dominant_topic"] = topic_weights.argmax(axis=1) + 1
topic_counts = negative_reviews["dominant_topic"].value_counts().sort_index()
topic_count_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "topic": topic_counts.index,
    "negative_reviews": topic_counts.values,
    "interpretive_label": [TOPIC_LABELS[number] for number in topic_counts.index],
})
display(topic_count_table)

Interpretation¶

The unsupervised topics independently recover complaint areas that are useful to management: repair and warranty failures, appointment problems, unanswered communication, customer-service conduct, property-management disputes, and moving or cleaning outcomes. This agreement between n-grams, rule-based aspects, and NMF strengthens the business case for a multi-part NLP solution.

6.4 Time patterns¶

The final year in the file contains only part of January 2022, so the trend chart ends at 2021. Years with very few reviews are shown in the table but should not receive equal interpretive weight.

In [25]:
df["review_year"] = df["date"].dt.year

yearly_summary = (

6.5 Business-level signal sufficiency¶

Individual-review classification can use every valid review. Business-level summaries require more evidence. The table below uses a minimum of 20 reviews and a Wilson lower confidence bound so a provider with a small number of negative reviews does not automatically rank above a provider with substantial evidence. Provider names are anonymized because this assignment evaluates the method, not individual companies.

In [26]:
def wilson_lower_bound(negative_count, total_count, z=1.96):
    if total_count == 0:
        return np.nan
    proportion = negative_count / total_count
    denominator = 1 + (z ** 2) / total_count
    center = proportion + (z ** 2) / (2 * total_count)
    margin = z * math.sqrt(
        (proportion * (1 - proportion) / total_count) + (z ** 2) / (4 * total_count ** 2)
    )
    return (center - margin) / denominator

business_summary = (
    df.groupby("business_id")
      .agg(
          provider_code=("provider_code", "first"),
          service_group=("service_group", "first"),
          reviews=("review_id", "size"),
          negative_count=("review_stars", lambda values: int((values <= 2).sum())),
          average_stars=("review_stars", "mean"),
          latest_review=("date", "max"),
      )
      .reset_index(drop=True)
)
business_summary["negative_rate"] = business_summary["negative_count"] / business_summary["reviews"]
business_summary["negative_rate_wilson_lower"] = business_summary.apply(
    lambda row: wilson_lower_bound(row["negative_count"], row["reviews"]), axis=1
)

threshold_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Minimum reviews": [10, 20, 30],
    "Eligible businesses": [
        int((business_summary["reviews"] >= threshold).sum()) for threshold in [10, 20, 30]
    ]
})
display(threshold_table)

# Determine the most frequently matched aspect for each business.
aspect_counts_by_business = df.groupby("business_id")[aspect_columns].sum()
max_aspect_column = aspect_counts_by_business.idxmax(axis=1)
max_aspect_count = aspect_counts_by_business.max(axis=1)
column_to_label = {
    "aspect_" + re.sub(r"\W+", "_", aspect.lower()).strip("_"): aspect
    for aspect in RISK_PHRASES
}
top_aspect = max_aspect_column.map(column_to_label)
top_aspect[max_aspect_count == 0] = "No dictionary match"

business_summary["top_matched_aspect"] = business_summary["provider_code"].map(
    dict(zip(
        df.drop_duplicates("business_id")["provider_code"],
        df.drop_duplicates("business_id")["business_id"].map(top_aspect)
    ))
)

eligible_businesses = business_summary[business_summary["reviews"] >= 20].copy()
review_signal_table = (
    eligible_businesses
    .sort_values(["negative_rate_wilson_lower", "reviews"], ascending=[False, False])
    [[
        "provider_code", "service_group", "reviews", "average_stars", "negative_rate",
        "negative_rate_wilson_lower", "top_matched_aspect", "latest_review"
    ]]
    .head(12)
)

6.6 Preliminary supervised text-classification feasibility test¶

This is a lightweight baseline—not the final tuned model. It tests whether text can distinguish clear negative-risk reviews from positive reviews.

Methodological safeguards:

  • Three-star reviews are excluded from this binary feasibility test.
  • URLs, emails, phone numbers, exact money values, and explicit star phrases are masked.
  • Exact normalized duplicate text is removed.
  • Entire businesses, rather than random rows, are held out with GroupShuffleSplit, preventing provider-specific language from appearing in both training and testing.
  • Class weights reduce the effect of the remaining label imbalance.
In [27]:
model_df = df[df["review_stars"] != 3].copy()
model_df["normalized_model_text"] = (
    model_df["model_text"].str.lower().str.replace(r"\s+", " ", regex=True).str.strip()
)
model_df = model_df.drop_duplicates(subset="normalized_model_text").copy()
model_df["target_negative"] = (model_df["review_stars"] <= 2).astype(int)

group_split = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.20, random_state=RANDOM_SEED)
train_index, test_index = next(
    group_split.split(model_df, model_df["target_negative"], groups=model_df["business_id"])
)
train_df = model_df.iloc[train_index].copy()
test_df = model_df.iloc[test_index].copy()

vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(
    lowercase=True,
    strip_accents="unicode",
    stop_words="english",
    ngram_range=(1, 2),
    min_df=3,
    max_df=0.95,
    max_features=35000,
    sublinear_tf=True,
)

X_train = vectorizer.fit_transform(train_df["model_text"])
X_test = vectorizer.transform(test_df["model_text"])

baseline_model = LogisticRegression(
    class_weight="balanced",
    max_iter=1000,
    solver="liblinear",
    random_state=RANDOM_SEED,
)
baseline_model.fit(X_train, train_df["target_negative"])

negative_probability = baseline_model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
baseline_prediction = (negative_probability >= 0.50).astype(int)

print(f"Training reviews: {len(train_df):,}")
print(f"Test reviews: {len(test_df):,}")
print(f"Training businesses: {train_df['business_id'].nunique():,}")
print(f"Held-out businesses: {test_df['business_id'].nunique():,}")
print("Business overlap:", len(set(train_df["business_id"]) & set(test_df["business_id"])))

# Error analysis uses masked excerpts and no provider names.
error_table = test_df[["provider_code", "review_stars", "model_text"]].copy()
error_table["actual_negative"] = test_df["target_negative"].values
error_table["predicted_negative"] = baseline_prediction
error_table["negative_probability"] = negative_probability
error_table["error_type"] = np.select(
    [
        (error_table["actual_negative"] == 1) & (error_table["predicted_negative"] == 0),
        (error_table["actual_negative"] == 0) & (error_table["predicted_negative"] == 1),
    ],
    ["False negative", "False positive"],
    default="Correct",
)

error_groups = []
for error_type, group in error_table[error_table["error_type"] != "Correct"].groupby("error_type"):
    sampled_group = group.sample(min(3, len(group)), random_state=RANDOM_SEED).copy()
    error_groups.append(sampled_group)

sampled_errors = pd.concat(error_groups, ignore_index=True) if error_groups else pd.DataFrame(
    columns=error_table.columns
)
sampled_errors["masked_excerpt"] = sampled_errors["model_text"].str.slice(0, 320)

display(sampled_errors[[
    "error_type", "provider_code", "review_stars", "negative_probability", "masked_excerpt"
]])

Interpretation¶

The business-held-out TF-IDF model substantially outperforms the lexicon benchmark, showing that review language contains strong predictive signal beyond individual keywords. The high score should not be treated as the final business solution: star ratings are directly expressed through customer language, and sentiment alone does not explain which operational issue management should fix. Error analysis also shows why mixed narratives and indirect complaints remain difficult.

Key exploratory findings¶

  1. Sufficient NLP corpus: the core subset contains 17,943 reviews from 1,054 home-service businesses, with about 2.07 million word tokens and a median of roughly 83 words per review.
  2. Useful negative evidence: the subset contains 5,994 reviews rated 1–2 stars, providing enough examples for risk-oriented text classification and theme discovery.
  3. Operational language is visible: negative n-grams emphasize unanswered calls, delays, warranty problems, and warnings to other customers; positive language emphasizes quality, timeliness, professionalism, and fair pricing.
  4. Service context matters: observed negative rates vary sharply by service group, so provider monitoring should use peer context rather than a single global threshold.
  5. Simple sentiment is insufficient: TextBlob follows star direction but misses many negative narratives, supporting a trained contextual model.
  6. Multiple methods converge: spaCy phrase matching and NMF both reveal communication, scheduling, professionalism, repair, warranty, and property-management themes.
  7. Business-level monitoring is feasible: 254 providers have at least 20 reviews in the analytical subset, enough for a cautious dashboard with uncertainty adjustment.
  8. Model feasibility is strong: a leakage-masked TF-IDF baseline evaluated on entirely held-out businesses achieves strong macro-F1 and negative-class recall, demonstrating that the text supports the proposed next stage.
  9. Responsible treatment is required: the data are historical, Tucson-specific, self-selected, and based on unverified customer accounts. Outputs must be labeled as review-based signals rather than verified violations or financial-failure predictions.

7. Proposed AI Solution (10%)¶

Proposed system¶

The next stage will create an explainable HomeLens Business Risk Intelligence pipeline:

Yelp review text
      ↓
PII, money, URL, and rating-phrase masking
      ↓
Sentiment / negative-risk classification
      ↓
Business-risk aspect detection
      ↓
Evidence-sentence extraction
      ↓
Provider-level aggregation with time and uncertainty
      ↓
Management dashboard and recommended investigation priority

Model comparison¶

  1. Lexicon baseline: TextBlob and optional NLTK VADER.
  2. Classical baseline: TF-IDF unigrams/bigrams with class-weighted Logistic Regression or Linear SVM.
  3. Transformer model: fine-tune distilbert-base-uncased using Hugging Face for negative-risk classification. DistilBERT is selected because it is smaller and faster than full BERT while preserving contextual language information.
  4. Aspect layer: begin with the transparent spaCy phrase matcher, manually annotate a stratified sample of negative reviews, and evaluate or fine-tune a multi-label aspect classifier if time permits.
  5. Business layer: aggregate review probabilities, repeated aspects, recent trend, review volume, and uncertainty. Require at least 20 reviews for published provider summaries.

Training and validation design¶

  • Mask direct rating phrases and PII before modeling.
  • Keep natural punctuation and word order for DistilBERT; do not stem transformer input.
  • Compare a business-held-out split with a chronological sensitivity test.
  • Tune thresholds on validation data rather than automatically using 0.50.
  • Preserve an untouched final test set.

Evaluation¶

Sentiment / negative-risk model¶

  • Macro F1
  • Negative-class precision, recall, and F1
  • Average Precision / PR-AUC
  • Confusion matrix
  • Performance by service group and review length

Aspect extraction¶

  • Human annotation of a review sample
  • Precision, recall, and F1 for each aspect
  • False-positive and missed-phrase analysis

Business dashboard¶

  • Minimum review threshold and Wilson or Bayesian smoothing
  • Recent versus prior negative-rate trend
  • Evidence sentences supporting each alert
  • No claim of bankruptcy, legal liability, fraud, or verified unsafe conduct

Expected business output¶

Provider: Provider_XXXX
Review-based risk tier: Elevated
Recent negative-review rate: increasing
Primary issue: Communication
Secondary issue: Workmanship
Evidence: masked customer sentence
Recommended management action: inspect callback procedures and repeat-repair cases

The proposed solution helps managers prioritize operational investigation, quality improvement, customer recovery, and reputation management. It does not replace human review.

8. Generative AI Use¶

Generative AI disclosure: The team used ChatGPT as a learning and productivity aid to help organize the notebook, troubleshoot Python code, suggest business-relevant NLP analyses and visualizations, and improve the clarity of written explanations. Official Yelp, spaCy, scikit-learn, NLTK, and Hugging Face documentation were consulted where applicable. All submitted code, outputs, analytical decisions, interpretations, and conclusions were reviewed and verified by the team. Generative AI supported the work but did not replace the team's responsibility to understand and explain it.

Final conclusion¶

The Yelp home-services corpus is an appropriate and competitive unstructured-data source for HomeLens AI. It contains enough natural-language detail and negative examples to support meaningful NLTK and spaCy exploration, supervised text classification, topic discovery, transformer fine-tuning, and business-level monitoring. The strongest business contribution is not merely predicting whether a review is negative; it is identifying the recurring operational issue, showing evidence, tracking change, and helping management decide what to investigate.
